'''Andrea Saltelli''' (born August 26, 1953, in [[Rome|Rome, Italy]]) is an Italian scholar specializing in [[Quantification (science)|quantification]] using [[Statistics|statistical]] and [[Sociology|sociological]] tools. He has extended the theory of [[sensitivity analysis]] to [[sensitivity auditing]], focusing on [[physical chemistry]], [[environmental statistics]], impact assessment and science for policy. He is currently Counsellor at the [[Pompeu Fabra University|UPF]] (Universitat Pompeu Fabra) [[:ca:UPF Barcelona School of Management]].

==Biography==
Saltelli earned his degrees in [[inorganic chemistry]] from [[Sapienza University of Rome]] in the summer of 1976. He then worked at the Italian Nuclear Authority [[ENEA (Italy)|ENEA]] and, for one year, at the [[Argonne National Laboratory]] in the [[United States]]. From 1992 to 2015, he worked at the [[Joint Research Centre]] of the [[European Commission]], leading a team dedicated to [[econometrics]] and [[applied statistics]] from 2005. Between 2016 and 2020, he held the position of associate [[professor]] at the Centre for the Study of the Sciences and the Humanities (Senter for vitenskapsteori) at the [[University of Bergen]].<ref>{{Citation |website=ORCID | title=andrea saltelli (0000-0003-4222-6975) | url=https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4222-6975 | access-date=15 March 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |website=Universitetet i Bergen | title=Andrea Saltelli | url=https://www4.uib.no/en/find-employees/Andrea.Saltelli | access-date=15 March 2024}}</ref>

==Sensitivity auditing==
In an interview for 'The Corbet Report',<ref name="Corbet">J. Corbett, "Interview 1424 – Andrea Saltelli on The Crisis of Science," The Corbett Report, 2019.</ref> Saltelli shared his early fascination with generating quantified evidence through statistical or mathematical [[model]]ling, highlighting his concern over how easy it is to produce poor-quality evidence, if not to manipulate data or [[Academic dishonesty|deceive with numbers]]. This concern drove his engagement with issues in the fields of [[epistemology]], [[philosophy of science]], and science for policy<ref name="Corbet"/> surrounding the responsible production of data.

This same concern led him to extend the theory of [[sensitivity analysis]] to [[sensitivity auditing]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lo Piano; Saltelli |first=Samuele; Andrea |date=September 2025 |title=Energy policy-making in the European Union between past and present |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2214629625003779 |journal=Energy Research & Social Science |volume=127}}</ref> which aims to assess the entire process of knowledge and model generation, including explicit or implicit assumptions, interests, stakes and motivations on part of the developers.<ref name="Latinorum">Saltelli, A., van der Sluijs, J., Guimarães Pereira, Â., 2013, Funtowiz, S.O., What do I make of your Latinorum? Sensitivity auditing of mathematical modelling, International Journal Foresight and Innovation Policy, 9 (2/3/4), 213–234.</ref> According to existing guidelines<ref name="SAPEA">Science Advice for Policy by European Academies, [https://www.sapea.info/topics/making-sense-of-science/ Making sense of science for policy under conditions of complexity and uncertainty], Berlin, 2019.</ref> including those from the [[European Commission]],<ref name="IA">European Commission, November  2021. [https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/law-making-process/planning-and-proposing-law/better-regulation-why-and-how/better-regulation-guidelines-and-toolbox_en Better Regulation: Guidelines and Toolbox]</ref> sensitivity auditing becomes particularly relevant when modelling results influence political decision-making processes.
